We Bought Copilot.
Then We Asked People to Show Us Last Tuesday.

Start with what people actually do with AI. Show what reaches leadership and what still needs manual coordination. Then explain how Nine-67 discovers the company-wide opportunities, prioritizes them, and builds a focused first pilot.

The fictional company

Northstar has 150 employees. Six people use AI in different ways. Leah, the chief of staff, turns their updates into a leadership view. This is an illustrative company, not a report of an actual client discovery.

How to present it

Josh runs the screen and asks the questions. Suuchi plays Northstar’s CEO during the opening, then answers as Nine-67’s CEO during the build discussion. Use one workspace at a time. The first half reveals the current state; the second half explains how we work.

0:00 - 0:50 · Scene 1Open scene 1

“We bought Copilot.”

Josh: Introduce fictional Northstar. Invite Suuchi to answer as its CEO.

Suuchi, as Northstar’s CEO: “I feel pretty good about where we are. Sales showed me something impressive last month. IT built an assistant for everyone. And personally? I use Claude before almost every board meeting.”

Josh: “If I spent a morning sitting beside your employees, what do you think I’d see?”

Do not treat a license purchase as proof of adoption or a lack of visibility as proof that people are doing something wrong. This is the beginning of discovery.

0:50 - 3:10 · Scene 2Open scene 2

Show us last Tuesday.

Josh: Visit the six workspaces. Spend roughly twenty seconds on each. Point to what the person puts in, what they get back, and where the result goes.

  1. Ava · Customer Service“Ava uses Copilot to get the tone of a customer email right. That is useful work. She still owns the customer response.”
  2. Ben · Sales“Ben uses Copilot with Excel to explore forecast slippage. He has developed something useful for his own sales review. We want to understand and preserve that.”
  3. Nina · Operations“Operations built AskOps inside Teams. It groups 18 tickets into three issues. This is a team-built capability the CEO has not seen.”
  4. Marcus · Account Management“Marcus uses personal Grok on his phone to rehearse a difficult conversation. His roleplay has no identifying client details. This is a different kind of AI use from editing a business record.”
  5. Daniel · IT“Daniel’s internal assistant retrieves policy information. He can explain the approved tool, but that does not give him a complete picture of everyone’s day-to-day AI use.”
  6. Suuchi · CEO“The CEO uses Claude to prepare for the board, working from the Friday updates Leah assembled. Claude helps her prepare from the material it receives.”

Josh: “There is real capability here. There is also no single view of how the company is using it.”

Keep the six uses distinct. Do not call them six integrated agents or suggest that every task should become an automated workflow. Marcus’s anonymized rehearsal is not an example of a data leak.

Optional research bridge: Miro’s 2026 survey reports that 83% agree AI improves individual productivity and 69% say most AI-assisted work happens in private sessions. Use those findings to frame the pattern, not to claim Northstar’s fictional activity was measured.

3:10 - 4:05 · Scene 3Open scene 3

What reaches the CEO?

Josh: Compare the work you just saw with the material that reaches the CEO’s Claude session. Follow the same people rather than introducing a second cast.

Josh: “The CEO is getting faster summaries. She is not necessarily getting the context behind each update, the links between departments, or the experiments people built for themselves.”

Suuchi, as Northstar’s CEO: “Claude helps me prepare. But it can only work with what reaches me.”

The problem is incomplete organizational context. Do not claim Claude should have silently accessed private chats or that a better prompt would reveal records it was never given.

4:05 - 5:00 · Scene 4Open scene 4

Leah’s Friday still looks familiar.

Josh: Show Leah comparing the updates and tracing which ones refer to the same underlying work. This is the human coordination cost.

Josh, quoting Leah: “Everyone gets their update to me faster now. I still spend Friday figuring out which updates are talking about the same thing.”

Josh: “People improved their own tasks. Leah still has to reconstruct the company-wide picture.”

Optional research bridge: Atlassian’s 2026 survey says 85% of knowledge workers use AI at work, while 29% have embedded it in their flow of work. This is why we look beyond tool adoption to the actual handoffs.

Do not assign invented hours or savings. Ask attendees to recognize the work: comparison, follow-up, ownership and reconciliation.

5:00 - 6:45 · Scene 5Open scene 5

“What would you actually do on Monday?”

Suuchi, as Northstar’s CEO: “Josh, I bought Copilot for everyone. I just learned my Ops team built a bot I’ve never seen, my sales director figured out forecasting on his own, and my chief of staff still spends Friday chasing updates. If I brought Nine-67 in on Monday, what would you actually do?”

Josh: Open the discovery inventory and opportunity map. Make the shift from the fictional company to Nine-67’s method explicit.

Josh: “First, we would look across the company. Sit with people, see the tasks they are doing, inspect the work they can share, and map the tools, systems, decisions and handoffs.”

Josh: “We would keep what is working, identify where the value stops at a department boundary, and prioritize opportunities by business value, feasibility, ownership and data access.”

Suuchi, as Nine-67’s CEO: “The discovery is broad. The first build is focused. We do not need to replace every tool or automate the whole company to prove a useful change.”

The deliverable is a company-wide view of current use and a prioritized build plan. Do not reduce the offer to inspecting just one workflow chosen in advance.

6:45 - 8:55 · Scene 6Open scene 6

Build one connection that finishes real work.

Josh: Run the focused service-to-account pilot. Show the manager’s review, the task assignment, the CRM context and the progress reaching the weekly review.

  1. Review the evidence“The workflow presents eight candidate cases. A service manager reviews them and excludes one unrelated case. Seven reviewed cases affect three accounts.”
  2. Assign the work“The reviewed issue goes to Nina with a named owner and due date. The system carries the source evidence and review decision with it.”
  3. Connect the account“Marcus sees the approved account context, owner and due date in the CRM. He does not have to reconstruct the service issue from another department’s conversation.”
  4. Close the loop“When progress changes, the weekly review receives that update. Leah can see the work and its ownership without rebuilding the same story on Friday.”

Suuchi: “The manager decides which cases belong together. Nina owns the follow-through. Marcus owns the account conversation. The workflow connects their work and keeps its status visible.”

The eight cases are candidates, not eight confirmed related incidents. The reviewed result is seven cases across three accounts. Do not present the pilot as a measured deployment or imply a live customer message was sent.

8:55 - 10:00 · Scene 7Open scene 7

Discover. Prioritize. Build. Measure.

Josh: “We discover how AI is being used across your company. Prioritize where connecting the work would matter. Build a focused pilot with the people who own it. Then measure what changed before expanding.”

Suuchi: “Who should they bring to the first conversation?”

Josh: “Bring operations, IT and leaders from two departments that depend on each other. Ask each person to bring one example of where AI helps today, and one piece of work they still have to chase.”

Q&A: what the discovery produces
  1. Current-use inventory. Who uses which tool for what task, the source information, the useful output and where the result goes.
  2. Handoff map. How work and decisions cross departments, where someone manually reconciles them, and who owns the next action.
  3. Prioritized opportunities. Compare business value, feasibility, permissions, source quality and accountable ownership.
  4. First-pilot plan. Define scope, human review, connected records, completion conditions, recovery paths and baseline measures before building.

Discovery uses authorized access and information people are permitted to share. It does not assume access to private AI histories or turn personal conversations into company records.

Q&A: what to measure

Agree on a baseline with the workflow owners. Potential measures include time spent coordinating, time waiting for a decision, missing ownership, repeated reconciliation and completion quality. Choose measures that match the pilot rather than claiming a universal saving.

The demonstration contains illustrative examples and simulated records. It provides no measured ROI, company benchmark, live incident classification or production integration result.

Research references and demonstration boundaries

Miro: State of Intelligent Collaboration 2026 supplies the 83% and 69% findings. Atlassian: State of Teams 2026 supplies the 85% and 29% findings. These are vendor-sponsored, self-reported surveys from different samples.

Northstar, its employees, their workspaces and the service cases are fictional. AI exchanges, approvals, CRM updates, assignments and weekly-review updates are simulated. No live account record or customer message is changed. The story is an illustration of the problem and a build approach, not evidence of a measured Nine-67 deployment.

Josh Lee hosts and runs the demo. Suuchi Ramesh plays Northstar’s CEO in the opening and explains Nine-67’s approach in the second half. The AI Workflow Discovery Session follows the webinar.
